Addison learned structures by building them, loading them, and checking them by hand.

The load path lesson

Straight fibers are a starting point. Real loads curve.

Composite material is only strong along its fibers. Textbooks lay fibers straight, at 0, 45, or 90 degrees. Force in a real part does not travel straight. It spreads from a mount and curves around shape changes. Two layups, side by side:

See it in the workSee it in the work

Conventional layup - fixed angles

Simple to make. Fibers cross the load instead of carrying it.

Steered fibers - follow the load

Harder to make. Material goes where the force goes.

Selected work

Three builds. One habit: check the work.

Open each marker for the full build: the claim, the steps, and what is actually true about the result.

How I work. Draw it first. Build it by hand. Check it twice. Write down what changed, so the next build starts from the truth.

My advantage

What a small crew teaches you

On a two-person crew and a student rocket team, there is no handoff to hide behind. You lay out the work, build it, and fix what your own checking finds.

That is the experience I bring to an internship team: real builds, checked in person, with the changes written down.

  • Hands-on from day one

    Every project here was built, not just modeled. The greenhouse is finished in Olympia, the rocket is a team build in progress, and the car is driven.

  • Checked work

    Square and brace, then check the diagonals again. Fit by hand first, then look again after a test. The second look is part of the job, not extra.

  • Full job, small crew

    Layout, framing, fitting, and fixing, all done by the same two people. A fast way to learn where a process is weak.

End-to-end process

The same loop on the rocket, the greenhouse, and the car

O1

Brief and constraints

Start from the real limits: the 4 in body tube the mount has to fit, the actual ground on site, the parts already on the car.

O2

Draw and lay out

Nothing gets built from memory. The rocket starts as a side profile with every section named. The greenhouse started as a site layout.

O3

Build and fit

Fit by hand first. A part seated without force is right. If it needs forcing, something upstream is wrong, and that gets fixed first.

O4

Review with the leads

The camera mount design was reviewed by Trevor Wong, Engineering Lead, and James Wolfe, Sub-Lead for Structures, before it went on the rocket.

O5

Test and inspect

The test is part of the build. Check the diagonals on the frame. Drive the car, then look again. A test you do not act on is just a delay.

O6

Fix and iterate

What the test shows changes the next version. Steer the design toward where the load actually goes, not where the first drawing put it.

O7

Write down what changed

What changed, and why, in plain words. That note is what the next build starts from, and how a lead can trust work they did not watch.

What I offer a team

I do not just model parts. I build them, and I check them.

Most students can show a model. I can show a finished greenhouse, a rocket airframe in progress with my team, and a car I maintain myself.

That means drawings grounded in how things actually go together, and notes a lead can rely on.

For a team, this means:

Drawings before building.

Every build starts drawn and named, so problems show up on paper first.

Fully checked fits.

Parts fitted by hand, tested, and inspected again after the test.

Changes on record.

What changed and why, written down for the next person on the part.

On paper only

  • Straight lines on a drawing
  • Assemble once and hope

Coursework - Autumn 2026

What I bring

Three courses this autumn at UW Tacoma, plus the training and habits behind the builds.

TME 221 - Statics

Forces, moments, and equilibrium. The direct link to structures work: if it does not balance on paper, it will not hold in real life.

TMATH 224 - Multivariable Calculus

Math in three dimensions: surfaces, vectors, and change across more than one variable at a time.

TMATH 207 - Differential Equations

How systems change over time, and how to model that change with equations you can actually solve.
